title: Queue Backpressure Cascade — Postmortem and Short Runbook
content:
Summary:

On 2025-01-09 18:23 PST a sustained surge of short, high-concurrency inference requests (median tokens < 8) landed on a subset of Dedicated GPU pools in us-west-2. The request pattern (many tiny calls at high qps) caused request queueing inside the allocator and continuous partial-batch formation that dramatically increased per-request latency and internal queue depth. The allocator and autoscaler signals interpreted the resultant GPU utilization patterns and request stalls as saturation and triggered several cascading mitigations (evictions, cluster-wide autoscale up/down oscillation) which amplified customer impact for ~42 minutes.

Why this is different from typical noisy-tenant cases:
- Not long-running heavy tensors or large memory allocations — requests were tiny but extremely bursty and poorly batchable given our current batching window heuristics.
- The root amplifier was queue backpressure inside the request router + a conservative eviction threshold combined with autoscaler hysteresis settings that cause overshoot when signal is noisy.

Incident timeline (UTC and local):
- 2025-01-09 01:23 UTC (18:23 PST): Alert: per-pool request latency increase (> p95) and request queue depth rising on pool-gamma-3
- 01:25: Pager to SRE rotation (Aisha) — initial slack investigation: dashboards show high pending_requests and low average batch_size (1.2)
- 01:27: Observed allocator logs: repeated Dequeue stalls + KV cache thrash logs from tenant t-981 (suspected noisy tenant)
- 01:30: Autoscaler saw aggregated GPU utilization drop (because GPUs were waiting on tiny batches and idle windows between micro-batches) and scheduled scale-down checks; autoscaler then rebalanced pods -> brief eviction of low-priority pods
- 01:33: Evictions cause additional task requeues; queue depth spiked cluster-wide due to cross-pool request reroutes
- 01:40: Manual mitigation: increased batching window to 25ms for affected pools and temporarily raised eviction thresholds; queue depth started to reduce
- 02:05: Traffic normalized; autoscaler returned to stable; root-cause analysis kickoff started

Immediate impact:
- ~7 customers routed through impacted pools saw p95 latencies increase from ~120ms to ~1.4s for 35 minutes
- A handful of low-priority background jobs were evicted and retried, causing duplicate retries in downstream systems

Root cause (hypothesis validated by logs and replay):
1) Traffic pattern: Many short requests arriving in bursts with high concurrency. Median tokens and compute per request were small so ideal behavior is short latency with small batches; but our continuous-batching policy has a 10ms window and a batch size floor that prevented efficient coalescing for these microbursts.
2) Queue amplification: Because average batch size stayed near 1, the router began building local queues per worker. Pending_request_count rose and request wait times increased.
3) Autoscaler misinterpretation: GPU utilization was noisy — GPU compute spent more time switching contexts and waiting for batches than executing long kernels. The autoscaler, using a 60s smoothing window on utilization and a conservative downscale policy, interpreted the noisy signal as capacity headroom and allowed downscales; that triggered pod moves and evictions.
4) Eviction cascade: Evictions requeued work and caused cross-pool routing which magnified queue depth and created positive feedback until manual interventions.

What went well:
- Telemetry surfaced two clear signals early: pending_request_count and average_batch_size.
- On-call playbook allowed quick change of batching window per-pool via console flag.
- Engineers coordinated with the product team to throttle known noisy tenant flows as an emergency mitigation.

Gaps and failures:
- Batching heuristics are not workload-adaptive: the fixed minimum batch size + short window assumption fails for microburst-heavy traffic patterns.
- Autoscaler rule set treats noisy utilization as safe to downscale because of the smoothing window; no separate signal for request queueing / backpressure existed in the autoscaler decision process.
- Eviction logic lacks an interlock with queue depth: we evict under the assumption of high utilization, but when queue depth is the problem, evictions worsen outcomes.

Short runbook (on-call checklist for similar events):
1) Triage:
   - Check pool metrics (affected pool id from alert): pending_request_count, avg_batch_size, p95 latency, gpu_utilization, eviction_rate
   - Quick command to list pools with high pending requests: kubectl get pods -l pool=dedicated -o wide --namespace=inference | grep -E "pending_requests>100" (replace with internal CLI)
2) Rapid mitigations (order matters):
   - Increase per-pool batching window to 25-50ms (temporary): set flag batching.window_ms=25 for pool X via console config or `rbctl pool update`
   - Increase batch size floor lower bound (allow 1 if needed) or switch to microbatch mode for that pool to avoid excessive packing attempts
   - Disable non-urgent evictions for the pool: set eviction.threshold=90% -> 95% temporarily
   - If specific tenant identified (t-981): throttle by applying tenant request rate limit and notify solutions-engineering to coordinate customer communication
3) Stabilize:
   - Monitor pending_request_count and avg_batch_size for 10 min intervals; if pending_requests trend down and latency improves, gradually revert flags back to defaults over 30 min
4) If autoscaler oscillation observed:
   - Pause autoscaler actions for affected cluster (suspend scale decisions) until queues clear
   - If automated pause is unavailable, scale cluster to +1 node temporarily and set autoscaler to manual for 10 minutes
5) Post-incident: open a follow-up ticket and capture all runbook steps

Longer-term actions (owners and TO-DOs):
- Batching: implement adaptive batching heuristics (owner: serving-runtime, Marco Chen) — target: detect microburst pattern and widen window dynamically; milestone Q1 2025
- Autoscaler: add queue-based signal into autoscaler decision logic (owner: platform-engineering, Priya Kapoor) — ensure autoscaler defers downscales if pending_request_count > X for pool
- Eviction policy: interlock eviction with queue depth and per-tenant behavior (owner: site-reliability-engineering, Leo Martínez)
- Monitoring: add a composite alert rule that fires when pending_requests > threshold AND avg_batch_size < 2 for > 30s. Create a dedicated dashboard tile for quick triage
- Customer controls: add tooling for emergency tenant-level rate limits from Console (owner: console-and-tooling)

Follow-ups opened (short ids):
- JIRA-4827: autoscaler-queue-signal (owner: Priya)
- JIRA-4831: adaptive-batching-prototype (owner: Marco)
- JIRA-4834: eviction-interlock-design (owner: Leo)

Open questions / unresolved:
- What threshold of pending_request_count should block downscale vs. just trigger a slower evaluation? Proposed: 50 requests/pool but needs SRE validation
- Should we make microbatch mode opt-in per-tenant or auto-detect? Cost/latency tradeoffs to evaluate

Appendix — useful commands & dashboards:
- Telemetry queries:
   - pending requests: metrics.pool.pending_request_count{pool=~"pool-gamma-.*"} by (pool)
   - batch size histogram: metrics.batch.size.histogram{model=~".*"}
   - GPU util vs idle: rate(gpu.kernel_time_seconds_total[1m]) / rate(gpu.uptime_seconds[1m])
- Emergency CLI snippets (internal tool `rbctl`):
   - Set batching window: rbctl pool set-config pool-gamma-3 batching.window_ms=25
   - Raise eviction threshold: rbctl pool set-config pool-gamma-3 eviction.threshold=0.95
   - Suspend autoscaler (if supported): rbctl cluster suspend-autoscaler us-west-2-dedicated

Notes to self (rough):
- We should run a synthetic microburst test matrix against staging pools to reproduce and tune heuristics before wide rollout
- Communicate with customer-success for affected tenants; prepare brief explanation and mitigation summary

Postmortem status: draft -> collecting logs and metrics attachment. Next sync scheduled with platform-engineering on 2025-01-16 to scope autoscaler changes.
